question: A 22-year-old college athlete reports intermittent exertional shortness of breath and cough only when playing soccer once weekly; she has no nocturnal symptoms, no activity limitation, and a small nasal polyp on exam. Which management choice best matches the recommended initial therapy for her condition?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the step-wise pharmacologic approach to treating asthma.

options.text: As-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with formoterol combination inhaler
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol for patients with minimal symptoms classified as mild asthma; this provides anti-inflammatory reliever therapy and reduces exacerbation risk.

options.text: Daily high-dose inhaled corticosteroid without a long-acting bronchodilator
options.rationale: Wrong because high-dose ICS is reserved for more severe disease; for mild asthma minimal therapy (low-dose ICS-formoterol as needed) suffices; this would be appropriate only if control remained poor on lower doses.

options.text: Short-acting beta agonist monotherapy as needed only
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture states SABA-only rescue is no longer recommended; as-needed SABA alone would be acceptable only if guidelines had not changed and the patient had no exacerbation risk factors.

options.text: Daily leukotriene receptor antagonist monotherapy
options.rationale: Wrong because leukotriene antagonists can be adjuncts but are not the preferred first-line single agent for mild asthma per the stepwise approach; it would be considered if ICS-formoterol were contraindicated or ineffective.

options.text: Daily tiotropium inhaler as sole maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because long-acting muscarinic antagonists are used as add-on therapy in more severe asthma; tiotropium alone would be inappropriate for initial management of mild asthma.

question: A 35-year-old man uses his rescue inhaler about four times weekly and had two emergency visits for asthma in the past year; he currently uses budesonide-formoterol only as needed. According to the lecture's classification and stepwise approach, what is the most appropriate change in his maintenance regimen?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the step-wise pharmacologic approach to treating asthma.

options.text: Begin scheduled low-dose budesonide-formoterol twice daily and continue as-needed use
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture classifies this as moderate asthma with increased exacerbation risk and recommends scheduled low-dose ICS-formoterol plus as-needed use (MART) to improve control and reduce exacerbations.

options.text: Increase as-needed budesonide-formoterol frequency only without scheduled dosing
options.rationale: Wrong because merely increasing as-needed use without scheduled maintenance does not address frequent symptoms and prior ED visits; scheduled maintenance plus reliever is recommended for moderate disease.

options.text: Switch to daily montelukast monotherapy and stop inhaled therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because montelukast is an adjunctive option, not preferred monotherapy for moderate asthma with prior exacerbations; it would be considered only if inhaled therapy were not tolerated.

options.text: Add tiotropium and discontinue inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol
options.rationale: Wrong because tiotropium is an add-on for more severe disease and cannot replace ICS; discontinuing ICS would increase exacerbation risk and contradict the lecture's stepwise approach.

options.text: Continue current regimen and prescribe oral antibiotics for prophylaxis
options.rationale: Wrong because antibiotics are not prophylactic asthma therapy; continuing inadequate control without stepping up maintenance contradicts the lecture guidance.

question: Which of the following historical features from the lecture most strongly predicts increased risk for future asthma exacerbations?
cited_learning_objective: To describe who is at highest risk for asthma exacerbations based on history.

options.text: Prior intensive care unit admission or endotracheal intubation for asthma
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists prior ICU admission or intubation as a major historical risk factor for future exacerbations.

options.text: Intermittent seasonal allergic rhinitis without prior exacerbations
options.rationale: Wrong because allergic rhinitis alone increases comorbidity risk but is not as strong a predictor as prior ICU admission or intubation; it would be more predictive if accompanied by prior severe exacerbations.

options.text: Remote childhood tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy
options.rationale: Wrong because prior T&A is not associated with increased exacerbation risk; it is listed in the case history but not as a risk factor for severe asthma.

options.text: Occasional viral bronchitis treated outpatient years ago
options.rationale: Wrong because a single remote outpatient bronchitis episode is not a major predictor; recurrent severe exacerbations are the concerning history.

options.text: Family history of seasonal allergies without personal exacerbations
options.rationale: Wrong because family history alone does not predict future exacerbations unless the patient has personal severe disease features.

question: A patient with asthma has pale, edematous nasal mucosa, posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning, and eczematous skin changes. Which concept from the lecture best explains the clustering of these findings?
cited_learning_objective: To define and describe the clinical presentations of commonly encountered obstructive lung diseases.

options.text: Atopic predisposition linking upper airway and skin allergic inflammation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, cobblestoning, and atopic dermatitis commonly coexist with asthma due to atopic inflammatory mechanisms.

options.text: Chronic bacterial sinus infection causing systemic inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic bacterial sinusitis may cause local symptoms but does not explain the presence of atopic dermatitis and nasal polyps characteristic of allergic disease.

options.text: Medication side effects from long-term inhaled beta agonists
options.rationale: Wrong because inhaled beta agonists do not cause nasal mucosal edema, cobblestoning, or eczema; these are features of allergic inflammation rather than drug adverse effects.

options.text: Autoimmune mucocutaneous disorder unrelated to airway disease
options.rationale: Wrong because autoimmune disorders would present differently and are not described in the lecture as commonly associated with asthma findings.

options.text: Occupational irritant exposure causing contact dermatitis and rhinitis
options.rationale: Wrong because occupational irritants could cause rhinitis or dermatitis but would not typically produce the constellation of nasal polyps, cobblestoning, and atopic dermatitis linked to atopy.

question: A 42-year-old woman hospitalized for an asthma exacerbation uses inhaled budesonide-formoterol twice daily plus as-needed doses but continues to have frequent symptoms and recent admission. According to the lecture's proposed classification, which adjustment is recommended next?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the most recent reclassification of asthma and appropriate step-up therapy.

options.text: Increase to high-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol and add montelukast and tiotropium
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends escalating to higher-dose ICS-formoterol and adding montelukast and tiotropium for severe uncontrolled asthma with frequent exacerbations.

options.text: Stop inhaled corticosteroid and switch to high-dose SABA monotherapy
options.rationale: Wrong because SABA monotherapy is no longer recommended and stopping ICS would worsen control; this contradicts the lecture's stepwise escalation.

options.text: Add daily oral antibiotics for chronic suppression
options.rationale: Wrong because antibiotics are not part of asthma maintenance therapy; they would be considered only for documented bacterial infection, not uncontrolled asthma per lecture guidance.

options.text: Replace inhaled therapy with montelukast monotherapy
options.rationale: Wrong because montelukast is an adjunct and cannot replace high-dose ICS in severe uncontrolled asthma; it would be insufficient alone.

options.text: Decrease inhaled corticosteroid dose and add intermittent systemic steroids
options.rationale: Wrong because decreasing ICS would likely worsen control; intermittent systemic steroids are for exacerbations, not a substitute for adequate maintenance dosing.

question: Which physical exam finding emphasized in the lecture most specifically suggests lower airway obstruction rather than an upper airway source?
cited_learning_objective: To define and describe the clinical presentations of commonly encountered obstructive lung diseases.

options.text: High-pitched expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes a high-pitched, musical expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiratory phase as characteristic of lower airway obstruction in asthma, distinct from transmitted upper airway sounds.

options.text: Noisy inspiratory stridor heard over the neck
options.rationale: Wrong because inspiratory stridor over the neck suggests upper airway obstruction, which the lecture warns can be confused with wheeze transmitted to the lungs.

options.text: Pale, edematous nasal mucosa with clear discharge
options.rationale: Wrong because nasal mucosal changes indicate allergic rhinitis, an upper airway finding, not direct evidence of lower airway obstruction.

options.text: Cobblestoning of the posterior pharynx
options.rationale: Wrong because posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning reflects chronic postnasal drip and allergic rhinitis, not lower airway obstruction.

options.text: Enlarged cervical lymph nodes with tracheal deviation
options.rationale: Wrong because cervical adenopathy and tracheal deviation suggest structural or infectious processes in the neck, not the typical lower airway wheeze described in asthma.

question: A patient with mild asthma is counseled about inhaler technique. The lecture emphasizes prescribing which adjunct device to improve medication delivery and technique?
cited_learning_objective: To describe integrating smoking cessation into management and inhaler technique importance (lecture emphasized inhaler teaching).

options.text: A spacer device to use with the metered-dose inhaler
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explicitly advises prescribing a spacer and teaching inhaler technique to improve delivery and reduce poor technique-related failures.

options.text: A peak flow meter for daily home spirometry
options.rationale: Wrong because while peak flow meters can monitor control, the lecture specifically highlighted spacers for improving inhaler technique rather than peak flow as the primary adjunct.

options.text: A nebulizer for all routine maintenance dosing
options.rationale: Wrong because nebulizers are not recommended for routine maintenance in place of inhalers; they may be used for acute relief but not as the standard adjunct for technique.

options.text: An oral spacer tablet to enhance systemic absorption
options.rationale: Wrong because no oral spacer tablets exist; this option is inconsistent with the lecture and would not improve inhaler technique.

options.text: A transdermal patch delivering beta agonist continuously
options.rationale: Wrong because transdermal beta agonist patches are not part of asthma management discussed in the lecture and would not address inhaler technique issues.

question: Which exposure listed in the lecture is identified as a trigger that increases risk for asthma exacerbations and should be addressed in management?
cited_learning_objective: To describe integrating smoking cessation into the management of all patients with obstructive lung disease.

options.text: Active cigarette smoking and second-hand smoke exposure
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists smoking and second-hand smoke as exposures that increase exacerbation risk and should be targeted in management.

options.text: Daily moderate exercise without environmental exposure
options.rationale: Wrong because exercise itself is not listed as an exposure increasing exacerbation risk unless associated with triggers; the lecture did not recommend avoiding exercise generally.

options.text: Routine childhood vaccinations
options.rationale: Wrong because vaccinations are not triggers for exacerbations and are not listed as exposures to avoid in the lecture.

options.text: Use of inhaled corticosteroids as maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because inhaled corticosteroids are protective maintenance therapy, not an exposure that increases exacerbation risk.

options.text: Daily consumption of dairy products
options.rationale: Wrong because dairy intake is not identified in the lecture as an exposure that increases asthma exacerbation risk.

question: A 32-year-old woman with severe, treatment-refractory asthma has frequent hospitalizations and prior intubations despite high-dose inhaled therapy. The lecture suggests which next step for patients with this profile?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the most recent reclassification of asthma and when to refer for expert assessment and add-on treatments.

options.text: Refer for expert assessment and consider biologic therapy such as anti-IgE monoclonal antibody
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends expert consultation and consideration of add-on treatments like omalizumab (anti-IgE) for severe asthma uncontrolled on maximal inhaled therapy.

options.text: Increase oral prednisone to chronic daily high-dose therapy indefinitely
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic high-dose systemic steroids carry significant adverse effects; the lecture advises specialist referral and targeted add-on therapies rather than indefinite high-dose oral steroids.

options.text: Discontinue all inhaled medications and trial of inhaled antibiotics
options.rationale: Wrong because stopping inhaled anti-inflammatory therapy would worsen control; inhaled antibiotics are not recommended for severe asthma without infection per the lecture.

options.text: Switch to SABA-only rescue therapy and observe outpatient
options.rationale: Wrong because SABA-only therapy is no longer recommended and would be inappropriate for severe, refractory disease; specialist evaluation is required.

options.text: Advise complete avoidance of all pets and environmental allergens without further therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because while allergen avoidance may help, it is insufficient alone for severe refractory asthma; the lecture emphasizes escalation of pharmacologic therapy and expert referral.

question: Which spirometric test result from the lecture is specifically associated with higher risk for asthma exacerbations?
cited_learning_objective: To describe who is at highest risk for asthma exacerbations based on test results.

options.text: Forced expiratory volume in one second less than 60% of predicted
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists FEV1  urban pattern.

options.text: Asthma prevalence is highest in elderly adults only
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture shows prevalence across age groups with notable rates in children and adults, not exclusively highest in the elderly.

question: A clinician is assessing asthma control using the lecture's symptom criteria. Which combination of symptom frequency would classify a patient as 'partly controlled'?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the new classification of asthma severity based on symptoms and risk.

options.text: One or two of the following daytime symptoms, nighttime awakenings, SABA use, or activity limitation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines 'partly controlled' as presence of one or two of the listed symptom criteria.

options.text: None of the symptom criteria present
options.rationale: Wrong because absence of all criteria corresponds to 'well-controlled', not 'partly controlled'.

options.text: Three or four of the symptom criteria present
options.rationale: Wrong because three or four criteria indicate 'uncontrolled' asthma per the lecture.

options.text: Only nocturnal awakenings without daytime symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong because a single symptom (nocturnal awakening) fits 'partly controlled' only if accompanied by none or one other; the option is too specific and not the lecture's general definition.

options.text: Daily SABA use with no other symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong because SABA use more than twice per week is one criterion; daily use alone could be one criterion but the lecture defines 'partly controlled' as one or two criteria, so the option is incomplete as a general rule.

question: A 40-year-old with asthma has frequent exacerbations despite medium-dose ICS-formoterol and has nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity. Which comorbid condition from the lecture is most relevant to her exacerbation risk and management?
cited_learning_objective: To describe comorbid diseases that increase risk for asthma exacerbations.

options.text: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with nasal polyposis
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease and nasal polyps as comorbidities that increase exacerbation risk and influence management.

options.text: Isolated hypertension without respiratory symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong because hypertension is not listed in the lecture as a comorbidity that increases asthma exacerbation risk.

options.text: Chronic kidney disease stage 3
options.rationale: Wrong because CKD is not emphasized in the lecture as a common asthma comorbidity affecting exacerbation risk.

options.text: Well-controlled hypothyroidism on replacement therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because well-controlled hypothyroidism is not identified in the lecture as a risk factor for asthma exacerbations.

options.text: Remote history of appendectomy
options.rationale: Wrong because prior appendectomy is unrelated to asthma exacerbation risk per the lecture.

question: A patient with mild asthma is prescribed budesonide 80 mcg/formoterol 4.5 mcg per puff to use one puff every four hours as needed. Which lecture-based rationale explains this dosing strategy?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the step-wise pharmacologic approach to treating asthma and rationale for as-needed ICS-formoterol.

options.text: Provides anti-inflammatory reliever therapy reducing exacerbations compared with SABA alone
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol acts as an anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR) and reduces severe exacerbations versus SABA-only rescue.

options.text: Maximizes systemic steroid exposure to prevent all symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong because the goal is to provide inhaled anti-inflammatory effect with minimal systemic steroid exposure; maximizing systemic steroids is not the lecture's rationale.

options.text: Is intended to replace maintenance therapy in all moderate and severe cases
options.rationale: Wrong because as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol is recommended for mild asthma and as part of MART for higher steps, but it does not universally replace maintenance in all moderate/severe cases without further adjustments.

options.text: Acts primarily as a mucolytic to clear secretions
options.rationale: Wrong because budesonide-formoterol provides anti-inflammatory and bronchodilator effects, not mucolytic action; mucolytics are not discussed in the lecture as the mechanism.

options.text: Is used to induce tolerance to inhaled allergens
options.rationale: Wrong because the combination is not an immunotherapy; it treats inflammation and bronchoconstriction rather than inducing allergen tolerance.

question: A clinician evaluates a patient with asthma and notes high short-acting bronchodilator use and incorrect inhaler technique. According to the lecture, which immediate action should the clinician prioritize?
cited_learning_objective: To describe integrating inhaler technique teaching into management of asthma.

options.text: Provide inhaler technique education and prescribe a spacer if using a metered-dose inhaler
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes teaching proper inhaler technique and prescribing a spacer to address poor technique and reduce exacerbation risk.

options.text: Discontinue inhaled corticosteroid and rely solely on oral therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because stopping inhaled corticosteroids would worsen control; the lecture recommends improving technique rather than discontinuing inhaled anti-inflammatory therapy.

options.text: Immediately start chronic oral antibiotics for prophylaxis
options.rationale: Wrong because antibiotics are not indicated for poor inhaler technique; the lecture does not support prophylactic antibiotics for asthma control.

options.text: Advise complete bed rest and avoid all physical activity
options.rationale: Wrong because activity restriction is not the primary intervention; improving inhaler use and adherence is the recommended immediate step.

options.text: Refer for surgical removal of nasal polyps before addressing inhaler use
options.rationale: Wrong because while nasal polyps may contribute to symptoms, the lecture prioritizes correcting inhaler technique and adherence as immediate, modifiable factors.

question: Which statement about the lecture's updated asthma classification is accurate regarding how severity is determined?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the most recent reclassification of asthma.

options.text: Severity is classified retrospectively after achieving control on the minimum effective therapy
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that asthma severity should be determined retrospectively once the patient is controlled on the minimum effective treatment.

options.text: Severity is based solely on initial symptom frequency at first presentation
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture emphasizes both symptoms and risk factors and recommends retrospective classification after treatment, not solely initial symptom frequency.

options.text: Severity is determined only by the number of inhalers prescribed
options.rationale: Wrong because medication count alone does not define severity; the lecture uses symptom control and exacerbation risk to classify severity.

options.text: Severity is fixed and cannot change with therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture indicates severity is dynamic and assessed after response to therapy, so it can change with treatment.

options.text: Severity is determined exclusively by presence of nasal polyps
options.rationale: Wrong because nasal polyps are a comorbidity that may increase risk but do not alone determine asthma severity per the lecture.

question: A 50-year-old patient with asthma has FEV1 55% predicted and frequent nighttime awakenings. According to the lecture, how would these findings influence risk classification and management intensity?
cited_learning_objective: To describe integrating symptom frequency and lung function into risk assessment and treatment escalation.

options.text: FEV1 < 60% and nocturnal symptoms indicate increased exacerbation risk and warrant escalation of anti-inflammatory therapy
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists FEV1 < 60% predicted and nocturnal awakenings as markers of increased risk, prompting step-up in maintenance anti-inflammatory therapy.

options.text: Normal lung function despite symptoms suggests no change in therapy is needed
options.rationale: Wrong because the presence of impaired FEV1 and nocturnal symptoms specifically indicate increased risk; normal lung function would not apply here.

options.text: Nocturnal symptoms alone require only SABA as-needed without changing maintenance
options.rationale: Wrong because nocturnal symptoms are one of the control criteria and may necessitate escalation of maintenance therapy rather than SABA-only management.

options.text: FEV1 55% predicts low exacerbation risk and allows de-escalation
options.rationale: Wrong because FEV1 below 60% predicts higher, not lower, exacerbation risk; de-escalation would be inappropriate.

options.text: Recommend immediate surgical intervention for nasal polyps to normalize FEV1
options.rationale: Wrong because while nasal polyp management may help symptoms, the lecture emphasizes pharmacologic escalation for impaired lung function and nocturnal symptoms rather than immediate surgery.

question: Which of the following is a lecture-identified comorbidity that can worsen asthma control and should be screened for during follow-up?
cited_learning_objective: To describe comorbid diseases that increase risk for asthma exacerbations.

options.text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists GERD as a comorbidity associated with increased risk for asthma exacerbations.

options.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.rationale: Wrong because type 1 diabetes is not listed in the lecture as a common comorbidity that increases asthma exacerbation risk.

options.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.rationale: Wrong because BPH is unrelated to asthma control and is not mentioned as a comorbidity in the lecture.

options.text: Osteoarthritis of the knee
options.rationale: Wrong because osteoarthritis is not identified in the lecture as a comorbidity that worsens asthma control.

options.text: Chronic hepatitis B infection
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic hepatitis B is not discussed in the lecture as a comorbidity affecting asthma exacerbation risk.

question: A 30-year-old with mild asthma and a small nasal polyp asks why nasal findings are relevant. Based on the lecture, which explanation best links nasal polyps to asthma management?
cited_learning_objective: To define and describe the clinical presentations of commonly encountered obstructive lung diseases.

options.text: Nasal polyps often indicate chronic upper airway allergic inflammation that coexists with lower airway asthma and may increase exacerbation risk
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes nasal polyps and chronic rhinosinusitis are commonly seen with asthma and can contribute to exacerbation risk and management complexity.

options.text: Nasal polyps are a sign of bacterial infection that directly causes bronchospasm
options.rationale: Wrong because nasal polyps reflect allergic/inflammatory processes rather than direct bacterial causes of bronchospasm per the lecture.

options.text: Nasal polyps indicate the need to stop inhaled corticosteroids immediately
options.rationale: Wrong because nasal polyps do not mandate stopping ICS; in fact, controlling upper airway inflammation may support asthma control.

options.text: Nasal polyps are unrelated to asthma and can be ignored in management
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture emphasizes the association between nasal polyps and asthma; ignoring them would miss a comorbidity that affects control.

options.text: Nasal polyps require systemic antibiotics to improve lung function
options.rationale: Wrong because systemic antibiotics are not the standard treatment for nasal polyps related to allergic disease; management focuses on anti-inflammatory strategies.

question: A 45-year-old with asthma uses albuterol frequently and has poor access to care. According to the lecture, which social factor increases risk for exacerbations and should be considered when classifying severity?
cited_learning_objective: To describe how setting and access to care influence asthma risk classification.

options.text: Lower income or difficulty obtaining regular follow-up and medications
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists setting factors such as lower income and difficulty accessing care as contributors to increased exacerbation risk and part of risk assessment.

options.text: Having a college degree and stable employment
options.rationale: Wrong because higher socioeconomic stability is not listed as increasing risk; the lecture highlights low-income settings as risk-enhancing.

options.text: Living in a rural area with abundant outdoor space
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture does not identify rural residence per se as a universal risk factor; it emphasizes access to care and poverty status.

options.text: Owning a pet with no allergic history
options.rationale: Wrong because pet exposure may be a trigger if sensitized, but ownership alone without sensitization is not the specific social access factor emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Working in a healthcare setting
options.rationale: Wrong because occupation is not singled out in the lecture as the social determinant most associated with increased exacerbation risk compared with access and poverty.

question: A patient with mild asthma asks why SABA-only rescue is no longer recommended. Based on the lecture evidence, which explanation is most accurate?
cited_learning_objective: To describe changes in asthma treatment recommendations and rationale for avoiding SABA monotherapy.

options.text: SABA-only rescue lacks anti-inflammatory action and is associated with higher exacerbation risk compared with ICS-formoterol
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that SABA-only therapy does not address airway inflammation and trials show higher exacerbation rates compared with as-needed ICS-formoterol.

options.text: SABA causes permanent airway remodeling when used alone
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture does not claim SABA causes remodeling; the primary concern is lack of anti-inflammatory effect and increased exacerbations.

options.text: SABA is ineffective at relieving bronchospasm in most patients
options.rationale: Wrong because SABAs relieve bronchospasm but do not reduce inflammation; the lecture does not state they are ineffective for symptom relief.

options.text: SABA is contraindicated in patients with nasal polyps
options.rationale: Wrong because nasal polyps are not a contraindication to SABA; the lecture focuses on anti-inflammatory needs rather than specific contraindications.

options.text: SABA increases systemic IgE levels when used frequently
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture does not describe SABA increasing IgE; this is not the reason for moving away from SABA monotherapy.

question: A 60-year-old with asthma has persistent symptoms despite maximal inhaled therapy and is being considered for add-on biologic therapy. Which biologic mentioned in the lecture targets circulating IgE?
cited_learning_objective: To describe additional maintenance therapy options for severe asthma including monoclonal antibodies.

options.text: Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture names omalizumab as a monoclonal antibody that binds free IgE and is an option for patients with allergic severe asthma.

options.text: Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist
options.rationale: Wrong because montelukast is an oral leukotriene antagonist, not a monoclonal antibody targeting IgE; it is an add-on but not the biologic described.

options.text: Tiotropium, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist
options.rationale: Wrong because tiotropium is a LAMA bronchodilator, not an anti-IgE biologic; it is used as an add-on inhaled therapy.

options.text: Budesonide-formoterol combination inhaler
options.rationale: Wrong because budesonide-formoterol is an inhaled corticosteroid-LABA combination, not a monoclonal antibody targeting IgE.

options.text: Albuterol nebulizer solution
options.rationale: Wrong because albuterol is a short-acting bronchodilator and not a biologic; it does not target IgE.

question: A patient with mild asthma is being considered for as-needed budesonide-formoterol. The lecture cites trial data showing what approximate relative reduction in severe exacerbations compared with albuterol alone?
cited_learning_objective: To describe evidence that as-needed ICS-formoterol reduces emergency visits and hospitalizations.

options.text: About a 66% decrease in severe exacerbations with as-needed budesonide-formoterol
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture presents trial data showing approximately a two-thirds reduction in severe exacerbations with albuterol-budesonide compared with albuterol alone.

options.text: No measurable change in exacerbation rates compared with albuterol
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture reports a significant reduction in severe exacerbations with ICS-formoterol versus SABA, not no change.

options.text: A 10% increase in severe exacerbations with as-needed budesonide-formoterol
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture indicates a decrease, not an increase, in severe exacerbations with ICS-formoterol.

options.text: Complete elimination of all exacerbations in treated patients
options.rationale: Wrong because while exacerbations decreased substantially, they were not completely eliminated according to the trial data cited in the lecture.

options.text: A 200% increase in emergency visits with as-needed budesonide-formoterol
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture shows a reduction in emergency visits, not a dramatic increase; this option contradicts the presented evidence.

question: A patient with asthma presents with audible wheeze, tachypnea, and decreased air movement. The lecture lists several acute management steps. Which immediate respiratory support was used for the severe acute case described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: To describe acute management steps for severe asthma exacerbation.

options.text: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP) with supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture case describes immediate use of BiPAP with set inspiratory and expiratory pressures and supplemental oxygen to maintain target saturation in severe asthma.

options.text: Immediate tracheostomy at bedside without trial of noninvasive support
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture describes BiPAP use; tracheostomy is not an immediate first-line step and would be inappropriate without other measures.

options.text: High-flow nasal cannula alone without bronchodilator therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because while oxygenation is important, the lecture emphasizes BiPAP in the described severe case and bronchodilator therapy is also required.

options.text: Routine chest physiotherapy and expectoration techniques only
options.rationale: Wrong because chest physiotherapy alone is insufficient for acute severe asthma; the lecture details ventilatory support and bronchodilator/steroid therapy.

options.text: Immediate initiation of chronic inhaled corticosteroid without acute bronchodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because acute management requires bronchodilation and ventilatory support; chronic ICS initiation alone is not the immediate step in severe exacerbation.

question: A 34-year-old with uncontrolled asthma despite medium-dose ICS-formoterol has persistent symptoms and frequent exacerbations. The lecture suggests adding which inhaled long-acting bronchodilator as a maintenance adjunct?
cited_learning_objective: To describe additional maintenance therapy options including LAMA use in severe asthma.

options.text: Tiotropium, a long-acting muscarinic antagonist
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists tiotropium as an add-on maintenance medication for severe asthma when control is inadequate on ICS-LABA.

options.text: Albuterol as scheduled twice daily
options.rationale: Wrong because scheduled SABA is not recommended as maintenance; albuterol is a rescue agent, not a long-acting maintenance bronchodilator.

options.text: Oral theophylline as first-line add-on
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture does not recommend theophylline as a preferred add-on; tiotropium (LAMA) is the inhaled option highlighted.

options.text: Daily intramuscular epinephrine injections
options.rationale: Wrong because IM epinephrine is not a maintenance therapy for asthma and is not discussed in the lecture as an add-on option.

options.text: Nebulized hypertonic saline daily
options.rationale: Wrong because nebulized hypertonic saline is not a standard asthma maintenance therapy per the lecture and would not substitute for LAMA add-on.

question: A patient with mild asthma is being classified using the lecture's criteria. Which combination of medication and risk factors would exclude them from being labeled 'mild' despite minimal symptoms?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the proposed new approach to asthma classification and factors that increase risk.

options.text: No inhaled corticosteroid prescribed and FEV1 < 60% predicted
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that absence of prescribed ICS and impaired lung function (FEV1 < 60%) are risk factors that preclude classification as mild even with minimal symptoms.

options.text: Minimal symptoms and no comorbidities with normal lung function
options.rationale: Wrong because this scenario fits mild asthma per the lecture; lack of risk factors and normal lung function support a mild classification.

options.text: Minimal symptoms with good access to care and prescribed low-dose ICS
options.rationale: Wrong because prescribed ICS and good access reduce risk and support mild classification rather than excluding it.

options.text: Minimal symptoms with daily montelukast and no prior exacerbations
options.rationale: Wrong because montelukast use alone without other risk factors does not automatically exclude mild classification; the lecture emphasizes absence of risk factors for mild status.

options.text: Minimal symptoms with scheduled high-dose ICS and no other risks
options.rationale: Wrong because being on high-dose ICS suggests more severe disease historically; however, the lecture defines severity retrospectively after control on minimum effective therapy, so this option alone is not the specific exclusion cited.

question: A 29-year-old with asthma and allergic rhinitis asks which nighttime symptom frequency would indicate uncontrolled asthma per the lecture criteria. Which frequency meets the uncontrolled threshold?
cited_learning_objective: To describe symptom-based criteria for asthma control classification.

options.text: Nighttime awakenings due to asthma occurring more than twice per week
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists nighttime awakenings as one of the symptom criteria and three or four of the criteria (including frequent nocturnal awakenings) indicate uncontrolled asthma.

options.text: Nighttime awakenings once every two months
options.rationale: Wrong because infrequent awakenings would not meet the threshold for uncontrolled asthma; the lecture focuses on more frequent symptoms.

options.text: No nighttime awakenings at all
options.rationale: Wrong because absence of nocturnal symptoms suggests better control and would not indicate uncontrolled asthma.

options.text: Nighttime awakenings only when exercising vigorously
options.rationale: Wrong because awakenings tied solely to vigorous exercise are not the general uncontrolled pattern described; the lecture uses overall frequency as the criterion.

options.text: Nighttime awakenings every other week
options.rationale: Wrong because this frequency is less than the lecture's threshold for uncontrolled symptoms and would more likely be partly controlled depending on other criteria.

question: A patient with asthma is being considered for an ICS-LAMA-LABA single-inhaler combination for severe disease. Which combination listed in the lecture corresponds to that option and dosing frequency?
cited_learning_objective: To describe additional option for severe asthma maintenance therapy: ICS-LAMA-LABA combinations.

options.text: Fluticasone furoate 200 mcg/umeclidinium 62.5 mcg/vilanterol 25 mcg, one puff daily
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists this specific triple combination and dosing of one puff daily as an additional option for severe asthma maintenance.

options.text: Budesonide 80 mcg/formoterol 4.5 mcg, one puff daily
options.rationale: Wrong because budesonide-formoterol is an ICS-LABA combination used in other steps, not the ICS-LAMA-LABA triple combination described with umeclidinium and vilanterol.

options.text: Tiotropium 1.25 mcg two puffs daily as the only inhaler
options.rationale: Wrong because tiotropium alone is a LAMA add-on, not the specific triple-combination product and dosing cited in the lecture.

options.text: Fluticasone propionate 50 mcg alone, one puff daily
options.rationale: Wrong because single-agent fluticasone is not the ICS-LAMA-LABA combination listed in the lecture and would not match the triple therapy dosing.

options.text: Albuterol 90 mcg two puffs every four hours as needed
options.rationale: Wrong because albuterol is a SABA rescue inhaler and not the ICS-LAMA-LABA maintenance combination discussed for severe asthma.

question: A 33-year-old with severe asthma is hospitalized with respiratory failure and is on chronic high-dose inhaled corticosteroid. The lecture case notes mild Cushingoid facies. Which explanation from the lecture best accounts for this finding?
cited_learning_objective: To describe adverse effects and systemic consequences related to asthma therapies discussed in severe cases.

options.text: Chronic systemic corticosteroid exposure from repeated oral steroid courses causing Cushingoid features
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture's severe asthma case included prednisone tapers and frequent exacerbations requiring systemic steroids, which can produce Cushingoid facies from cumulative systemic steroid exposure.

options.text: Long-term use of inhaled beta agonists causing fat redistribution
options.rationale: Wrong because inhaled beta agonists do not cause Cushingoid fat redistribution; systemic corticosteroids are the typical cause as described in the lecture.

options.text: Chronic hypoxia leading to facial edema and Cushingoid appearance
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoxia does not produce classic Cushingoid facies; the lecture links steroid exposure to these features.

options.text: Omalizumab therapy causing steroid-like side effects
options.rationale: Wrong because omalizumab is an anti-IgE biologic and does not cause Cushingoid features; systemic steroids do.

options.text: Poor nutrition leading to moon facies
options.rationale: Wrong because malnutrition does not cause the characteristic steroid-induced moon facies; the lecture attributes this to systemic corticosteroid exposure.

question: A clinician is reviewing risk factors for asthma exacerbations. Which medication-related behavior from the lecture is most likely to increase exacerbation frequency and should prompt intervention?
cited_learning_objective: To describe medication-associated factors that increase risk for asthma exacerbations.

options.text: High reliance on short-acting bronchodilators with poor adherence to inhaled corticosteroids
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture identifies high SABA use combined with poor adherence to anti-inflammatory therapy as a medication-associated risk factor for exacerbations.

options.text: Consistent daily use of prescribed inhaled corticosteroids with correct technique
options.rationale: Wrong because adherence to ICS with correct technique reduces exacerbation risk rather than increasing it.

options.text: Occasional use of leukotriene antagonist as adjunct
options.rationale: Wrong because occasional adjunctive leukotriene antagonist use is not highlighted as a major exacerbation-promoting behavior in the lecture.

options.text: Use of spacer with metered-dose inhaler
options.rationale: Wrong because spacer use improves delivery and reduces risk; it is recommended, not harmful.

options.text: Regular follow-up with asthma specialist
options.rationale: Wrong because specialist follow-up typically reduces exacerbation risk by optimizing therapy; it is not a harmful behavior.

question: A 26-year-old with mild asthma and no comorbidities asks about the rationale for using a single inhaler for both maintenance and reliever therapy (MART). Based on the lecture, which statement best summarizes the advantage of this approach?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the step-wise approach and rationale for using ICS-formoterol as both controller and reliever.

options.text: Using one ICS-formoterol inhaler for maintenance and relief simplifies regimen and reduces exacerbations
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture highlights that a single inhaler used as maintenance and reliever (MART) simplifies treatment and lowers exacerbation risk compared with separate reliever strategies.

options.text: Single-inhaler MART eliminates the need for any anti-inflammatory therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because MART still delivers anti-inflammatory therapy via ICS; it does not eliminate the need for anti-inflammatory treatment.

options.text: MART is recommended only for patients who cannot use spacers
options.rationale: Wrong because MART is a therapeutic strategy based on evidence of reduced exacerbations, not limited to spacer inability.

options.text: MART increases systemic steroid exposure compared with separate inhalers
options.rationale: Wrong because MART aims to reduce systemic steroid exposure by providing inhaled anti-inflammatory reliever doses; the lecture does not state it increases systemic steroid exposure.

options.text: MART is only used in patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
options.rationale: Wrong because MART is a general strategy for many patients and is not restricted to aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease per the lecture.

question: A patient with asthma has frequent exacerbations and is being evaluated for severity. The lecture emphasizes assessing both symptoms and risk. Which of the following best represents the lecture's two-component framework for classifying asthma severity?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the new classification of asthma severity based on symptoms and risk of future exacerbations.

options.text: Current symptom control and risk of future exacerbations
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that severity classification should consider both current symptom frequency (control) and risk factors for future exacerbations.

options.text: Only the number of inhalers prescribed
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture rejects medication count alone as the basis for severity classification; it requires symptom and risk assessment.

options.text: Only the presence of nasal polyps
options.rationale: Wrong because nasal polyps are a comorbidity that may increase risk but do not alone define severity per the lecture.

options.text: Only the patient's age and sex
options.rationale: Wrong because demographic factors alone are insufficient; the lecture emphasizes symptoms and risk factors.

options.text: Only the number of prior hospital admissions regardless of current control
options.rationale: Wrong because while prior admissions inform risk, the lecture requires combining that with current symptom control to classify severity.

question: A 38-year-old with asthma reports frequent exposure to airborne irritants at work and uses his SABA multiple times daily. According to the lecture, which exposure-related recommendation should be prioritized to reduce exacerbation risk?
cited_learning_objective: To describe exposures/triggers that increase risk for asthma exacerbations and management implications.

options.text: Identify and reduce workplace airborne irritant exposure and optimize anti-inflammatory therapy
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists recurrent exposure to airborne irritants as a trigger and recommends addressing exposures along with optimizing pharmacologic control.

options.text: Advise complete avoidance of all outdoor air and confinement indoors
options.rationale: Wrong because blanket confinement is impractical and not recommended; targeted reduction of specific irritant exposures is the lecture's approach.

options.text: Recommend increasing SABA frequency as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Wrong because high SABA use indicates poor control and should prompt anti-inflammatory optimization and exposure mitigation, not increased SABA reliance.

options.text: Prescribe daily antibiotics to prevent irritant-induced exacerbations
options.rationale: Wrong because antibiotics do not prevent irritant-triggered asthma exacerbations and are not recommended in the lecture for this purpose.

options.text: Suggest switching to a different job without addressing inhaler adherence
options.rationale: Wrong because while job change may help, the lecture emphasizes addressing exposures and medication optimization together rather than only job change.

question: A 24-year-old with mild asthma and no prior exacerbations asks about the safety of as-needed budesonide-formoterol. Based on the lecture, which regulatory and guideline status best reflects this therapy?
cited_learning_objective: To describe guideline adoption and regulatory approval of as-needed ICS-formoterol.

options.text: Approved in many countries and recommended by multiple guidelines including GINA for mild asthma
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that as-needed ICS-formoterol has been approved in about 50 countries and is recommended in guidelines such as GINA for mild asthma management.

options.text: Not approved anywhere and universally discouraged by guidelines
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture states the opposite: it is approved in many countries and recommended by guidelines, not universally discouraged.

options.text: Approved only for pediatric use and not for adults
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture discusses adult and adolescent use and guideline recommendations, not exclusive pediatric approval.

options.text: Recommended only when oral steroids are contraindicated
options.rationale: Wrong because as-needed ICS-formoterol is a primary reliever strategy, not reserved solely for steroid contraindication scenarios per the lecture.

options.text: Banned in most countries due to safety concerns
options.rationale: Wrong because the lecture indicates regulatory approval and guideline endorsement rather than bans for safety concerns.

question: A patient with severe asthma remains symptomatic despite maximal inhaled therapy and frequent systemic steroid courses. The lecture suggests which specialist intervention to consider next?
cited_learning_objective: To describe when to refer for expert assessment and add-on treatments for severe asthma.

options.text: Refer for expert phenotyping and consideration of targeted biologic add-on therapy
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends expert assessment, phenotyping, and add-on treatments (e.g., omalizumab) for severe uncontrolled asthma despite maximal therapy.

options.text: Stop all inhaled therapies and begin long-term oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Wrong because stopping inhaled anti-inflammatory therapy and starting antibiotics is not the recommended approach; specialist evaluation for targeted therapy is indicated.

options.text: Initiate daily high-dose SABA nebulization at home
options.rationale: Wrong because frequent SABA use is associated with worse outcomes and is not recommended as a maintenance strategy per the lecture.

options.text: Recommend immediate lung volume reduction surgery
options.rationale: Wrong because surgical interventions like lung volume reduction are not standard for asthma management; the lecture advises specialist pharmacologic options first.

options.text: Advise complete cessation of all physical activity indefinitely
options.rationale: Wrong because activity restriction is not the primary management for severe refractory asthma; targeted medical therapy and specialist referral are preferred.

question: A 31-year-old with asthma uses budesonide-formoterol as needed and asks how the combination prevents exacerbations mechanistically. Which mechanism from the lecture best explains the benefit?
cited_learning_objective: To describe the mechanism by which ICS-formoterol as an anti-inflammatory reliever reduces exacerbations.

options.text: Provides rapid bronchodilation from formoterol plus immediate anti-inflammatory effect from inhaled corticosteroid at time of symptoms
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that formoterol gives quick bronchodilation while the inhaled corticosteroid delivers anti-inflammatory action when used as-needed, reducing progression to severe exacerbation.

options.text: Formoterol acts as an anti-IgE agent while budesonide increases mucus production
options.rationale: Wrong because formoterol is a LABA bronchodilator, not an anti-IgE agent, and budesonide is an anti-inflammatory corticosteroid, not a mucus-promoting drug; this contradicts lecture mechanisms.

options.text: The combination works by systemic immunosuppression equivalent to oral prednisone
options.rationale: Wrong because inhaled budesonide provides local anti-inflammatory effects with less systemic immunosuppression than oral prednisone; the lecture emphasizes inhaled anti-inflammatory reliever action, not systemic equivalence.

options.text: It functions primarily by increasing IgE production to neutralize allergens
options.rationale: Wrong because increasing IgE would worsen allergic responses; the lecture describes anti-inflammatory and bronchodilator effects, not IgE augmentation.

options.text: It prevents viral infections that trigger most exacerbations
options.rationale: Wrong because while reducing inflammation may blunt some viral-triggered worsening, the combination does not directly prevent viral infections; the lecture focuses on anti-inflammatory reliever effects.
